concepts.title: Progressive overload
concepts.hook: A heavy school bag can feel normal after a few weeks of carrying it. The bag did not change. What did?
concepts.rule: Muscles adapt to work they are not used to. To keep progressing, add weight, clean reps or training days, and keep each weekly jump small next to what you already do. Pain or shortness of breath means rest.

claims.text: Strength training improves muscle strength and size, and healthy adults are advised to make it progressive.
Strength work makes muscles do more work than they are used to. This is called overload, and the body adapts to it. Body weight, as in push-ups, can be the load.
Strength grows over time when the weight, the sets or reps, or the days a week of training go up bit by bit.
Small, steady rises in overload help the body adapt while keeping injury risk low. The size of each weekly rise, next to what you already do, is linked to injury risk.
Effort should rise gradually, and shortness of breath, pain, nausea or headache are signs the body needs rest.

items.stem: For two school years, Aisha carried a heavy bag up three floors of stairs. Why did it stop feeling heavy?

options.text: Her body adapted to the load she carried each day.
options.feedback: The daily bag was more than her body was used to at first, so it adapted and the load now feels normal.

options.text: Repeated carrying wore her muscles down.
options.feedback: The body adapts to work it repeats. That adaptation made the familiar load feel easier.

options.text: Carrying it so often wore her muscles out.
options.feedback: Repeated work made her body adapt, not wear out, which is why the same bag feels lighter.

items.stem: A gym friend says push-ups cannot build strength because they use no weights. What is not quite right?

options.text: Your own body weight is the load the muscles push.
options.feedback: Push-ups, pull-ups and planks count as strength work, because your body weight gives the muscles their load.

options.text: Push-ups help, but they need a year before any gain.
options.feedback: There is no one-year wait. Push-ups load the arm and chest muscles from the start.

options.text: Push-ups mostly train the heart, not the chest muscles.
options.feedback: Push-ups mainly work the chest, shoulders and upper arms against body weight, so they are strength work.

items.stem: At the college gym, Dev can row 8 kg only by swinging his back. His friend says to add more weight. What is the catch?

options.text: Swung reps are not clean work, so he should first make 8 kg clean.
options.feedback: Growing the work means clean reps with good form. Adding weight to swung reps adds risk, not useful work.

options.text: There is no catch, since more weight is the natural next step.
options.feedback: More weight helps only once the reps are clean. Swinging means the form is not there yet.

options.text: A big weight jump will make him stronger faster.
options.feedback: Large jumps raise injury risk. Small, steady rises help the body adapt.

items.stem: Nikhil kept the same weights and the same reps all term, yet he kept getting stronger. He must have added ___.

options.text: a training day each week.
options.feedback: If the load and reps stayed the same, the work grew through more days in the week.

options.text: longer rests between his sets.
options.feedback: Longer rests make each session easier, not bigger. With load and reps fixed, more days grew the work.

options.text: a faster pace on each rep.
options.feedback: Rushing reps does not add clean work. With load and reps fixed, an extra day is what grew.

items.stem: As progressive overload, Sameer adds a fourth 20-minute jog to his three a week. About what percent rise is that for the week?

options.text: About 33%.
options.feedback: Three 20-minute jogs make 60 minutes, so 20 more is a third, about 33%. That is a big jump for one week.

options.text: About 20%.
options.feedback: 20 is the extra minutes, not the share. 20 more on 60 is about a third.

options.text: About 100%.
options.feedback: That would double his week. One extra jog on top of three adds about a third.

items.stem: Why does the size of each weekly rise matter?

options.text: A rise that is big next to your usual amount is linked to injury.
options.feedback: Small, steady rises let the body adapt, while big jumps next to what you already do raise injury risk.

options.text: Small rises give too little gain, so big ones are better.
options.feedback: Small rises still give the body something new to adapt to. Big jumps add injury risk.

options.text: Big jumps build strength faster and add no extra risk.
options.feedback: Big jumps next to your usual amount are linked to more injuries, so they are not a free shortcut.

misconceptions.name: More weight every visit
misconceptions.correction: A gradual rise can use clean reps, load or days; it does not have to mean more weight each session.

misconceptions.name: Bigger jumps work faster
misconceptions.correction: The size of each weekly jump, next to your usual amount, is linked to injury risk.

misconceptions.name: Strength work needs weights
misconceptions.correction: Your own body weight can be the load, as in push-ups, pull-ups and planks.

misconceptions.name: Repeated work only wears muscles out
misconceptions.correction: The body adapts to repeated work, so the same load can come to feel easier.

steps.title: Overload means asking a bit more than usual

hook.stem: Ten push-ups felt hard a month ago and feel easy now. What changed?

options.text: Your muscles adapted to the work.
options.feedback: Right. Muscles adapt to work they are not used to, so the same task now takes less effort.

options.text: You are doing them faster and sloppier.
options.feedback: Speed and sloppy form are not the reason. Your muscles adapted, so the same push-ups feel easier.

options.text: Easy now means the training stopped working.
options.feedback: Easy is a sign it worked. Your muscles caught up with the load you kept giving them.

steps.teach: Asked to do a bit more than usual, a muscle adapts and gets stronger, so the same work feels easier next time. That push is called overload. Your own body weight can be the load.

parts: Meera usually does 8 squats in her hostel room,
today she does 9 with the same good form,
and in a few weeks 9 will feel normal.
example.spot: today she does 9 with the same good form,
example.feedback: One squat more than usual is the overload. Her legs adapt, so 9 soon feels normal.

guided.stem: Kunal has done the same 12 squats every day for three months, and he has stopped getting stronger. Why?
guided.hint: Ask what has changed in his routine.

options.text: His legs caught up, and nothing new is asked of them.
options.feedback: Yes. The same work stops being more than usual, so there is nothing new to adapt to.

options.text: Squats stop building strength after the first month.
options.feedback: Squats keep working when they grow. His just stayed the same for three months.

options.text: He needs a few months of full rest to grow.
options.feedback: Rest is not the missing piece. His legs need a little more than they are used to.

steps.takeaway: Muscles adapt when you ask a little more than usual.

steps.title: Keep progress going: add weight, reps or days

hook.stem: You can already do 15 clean squats and own no weights. What else can you change?

options.text: Add a few clean reps, or one more training day.
options.feedback: Right. More clean reps or an extra day a week grows the work, with no weights needed.

options.text: Nothing; without weights the work cannot grow.
options.feedback: Weights are one way, not the only way. Clean extra reps or an extra day also grow the work.

options.text: Do them faster, even if your form slips.
options.feedback: Sloppy reps do not add useful work. Clean extra reps or one more day a week do.

steps.teach: Once work feels easy, the body has caught up, so the work has to grow. Add a little weight, a few clean reps (good form), or one more training day a week.

parts: Kabir did strength work twice a week last term,
then added a third day this term,
and his lifts kept getting stronger.
example.spot: then added a third day this term,
example.feedback: Adding a training day raised his weekly work, so his strength kept rising.

guided.stem: Sana can do 12 clean lunges. Which change grows the work?
guided.hint: Which choice makes each lunge a bit harder?

options.text: Hold a water bottle in each hand.
options.feedback: Yes. The bottles add a little weight, so each lunge asks a bit more of her legs.

options.text: Do 12 lunges at half the depth.
options.feedback: Shallow lunges make each rep easier, so the work shrinks instead of growing.

options.text: Do 6 lunges instead, but much faster.
options.feedback: Fewer reps is less work, not more, and rushing them does not add clean work.

steps.takeaway: To keep improving, add weight, clean reps or a training day.

steps.title: Keep each weekly jump small

hook.stem: Who takes the bigger jump: going from 40 to 60 minutes a week, or from 200 to 220?

options.text: The one going from 40 to 60.
options.feedback: Right. 20 more minutes is a 50% jump on 40, but only 10% on 200.

options.text: The one going from 200 to 220.
options.feedback: Both add 20 minutes, but 20 on top of 200 is only a 10% rise.

options.text: Both, since the extra minutes match.
options.feedback: The minutes match, but the share does not. 20 is half of 40 and a tenth of 200.

steps.teach: Grow in small steps, because a jump that is big next to what you already do is linked to more injuries. Ten extra minutes is big on 40, small on 200. Pain means rest.

visual.label: Weekly rise in jogging time, next to your usual

parts: Isha jogs 100 minutes a week,
adds just 10 minutes the next week,
and keeps that new total for a while.
example.spot: adds just 10 minutes the next week,
example.feedback: Ten minutes on top of 100 is a 10% rise, a small step for her body.

guided.stem: Ravi runs 50 minutes a week. Which next week is the smallest jump for him?
guided.hint: Work out each rise as a share of what he does now.

options.text: 55 minutes.
options.feedback: Yes. 5 more on 50 is a 10% rise, a gentle step.

options.text: 75 minutes.
options.feedback: 25 more on 50 is a 50% rise, a big jump for one week.

options.text: 100 minutes, to get fit fast.
options.feedback: Doubling to 100 is a 100% rise, far bigger than the other choices.

steps.takeaway: Keep each weekly jump small next to what you already do.

concepts.title: Muscle, protein and rest
concepts.hook: Training gives muscle a task. Food and time between hard sessions help the body respond.
concepts.rule: Strength work is the signal to build and protein from food is the material. Healthy adults need about 0.83 g of protein per kilo a day, and more than about 1.6 g added no extra muscle. The building process can stay on for up to two days.

claims.text: India's food guide sets 0.83 g of protein per kg a day for healthy adults. In strength training, more than about 1.6 g per kg a day added no further muscle.
Strength work and eating protein both switch on muscle building, and together they do more than either alone. Without exercise, protein is not used to build muscle.
After one strength session, the muscle-building process can stay raised for up to 48 hours. The rise was smaller in adults over 50.
Most people who train can get enough protein from food alone, without powders. People with kidney disease should take care with high protein.

items.stem: In the hostel, Kabir trains his legs hard on Monday, eats well, and by Thursday they feel ready again. Working back, when did most of the building happen?

options.text: In the days after, while he rested and ate.
options.feedback: Right. Building stays switched on for up to two days after a session, and his meals fed it.

options.text: During the Monday session itself.
options.feedback: The session gives the signal. Building carries on for up to two days afterwards, fed by meals.

options.text: On Thursday, once his legs felt ready.
options.feedback: Feeling ready came after the work was done. Building ran in the days straight after Monday.

items.stem: A gym friend says you cannot build muscle without protein powder. What is not quite right?

options.text: Dal, eggs, milk or paneer can supply the protein.
options.feedback: Most people who train can get enough protein from food alone, so powders are not needed.

options.text: Powder is needed, at least on training days.
options.feedback: Food covers training days too. Most people who train get enough protein without powder.

options.text: Muscle grows from training, so protein hardly matters.
options.feedback: Protein does matter as the material. It just does not have to come from powder.

items.stem: Ravi has kidney disease and plans a very high-protein diet to build muscle. What does this step say about his plan?

options.text: Take care: high protein needs caution with kidney disease.
options.feedback: Right. The step flags high protein as something people with kidney disease need to take care with.

options.text: Go ahead, since more protein means more muscle.
options.feedback: Extra protein past about 1.6 g per kilo added no muscle, and with kidney disease high protein needs care.

options.text: Nothing changes, since kidneys do not affect protein.
options.feedback: The step names kidney disease as a reason to take care with high protein, so it does matter here.

items.stem: Your mother weighs 55 kg and does no muscle training. Estimate her daily protein need.

options.text: About 46 g.
options.feedback: 55 times 0.83 is about 46, and the same healthy-adult figure holds without any training.

options.text: About 55 g.
options.feedback: That uses 1 g per kilo. At 0.83 g per kilo, 55 kg needs about 46 g.

options.text: About 88 g.
options.feedback: That is 55 times 1.6, the point where extra stops helping. Her need is about 46 g.

items.stem: At college, Zoya has eaten dal and curd daily for years. This term she adds squats three times a week. What changes for her muscles?

options.text: The protein she eats now has a signal to build.
options.feedback: Right. Her food gave the parts all along, and the new training gives the signal, so now both work together.

options.text: Nothing, since her food already built muscle.
options.feedback: Without training, the body does not use that protein for muscle. The squats add the missing signal.

options.text: She must now stop eating dal on squat days.
options.feedback: Training does not replace food. The squats give the signal, and her dal and curd give the parts.

items.stem: Which line best explains why the time after training matters?

options.text: The muscle-building process can stay on for up to two days.
options.feedback: A review found the rise can last up to 48 hours after one session, so that time counts.

options.text: Muscles change while you lift, so the time after adds little.
options.feedback: The building process keeps going after the session, for up to about two days.

options.text: Muscle building starts once soreness ends.
options.feedback: Muscle building can stay raised for up to 48 hours after a session. It does not wait for soreness to end.

misconceptions.name: Powder is needed
misconceptions.correction: Food like dal, eggs, milk and paneer can supply the protein; powders are not needed.

misconceptions.name: More protein, more muscle
misconceptions.correction: Above about 1.6 g per kilo a day, extra protein added no more muscle.

misconceptions.name: Growth happens only in the gym
misconceptions.correction: The muscle-building process can stay switched on for up to two days after a session.

misconceptions.name: Muscle building waits until soreness ends
misconceptions.correction: Muscle building can stay raised for up to two days after a strength session.

misconceptions.name: Protein alone builds muscle
misconceptions.correction: Strength work gives the body a signal to use protein for muscle building.

steps.title: Training is the signal, protein is the material

hook.stem: Two friends eat the same dal and paneer. Only one also does strength work. Whose muscles get the bigger boost?

options.text: The one who also trains.
options.feedback: Right. Training and protein work together, so doing both gives more muscle building.

options.text: Both the same, since the food is the same.
options.feedback: Food alone helps less. Strength work adds the signal that tells muscle to build.

options.text: The one who rests, since rest lets muscle grow.
options.feedback: Without training there is no signal to build, so the protein is not used for muscle.

steps.teach: Strength work tells a muscle to build, and protein from food gives it the parts. Without the training, the body does not use that protein for muscle, so you need both.

parts: Ananya does squats and push-ups at 6 pm,
then eats rajma, rice and curd for dinner,
and sleeps well that night.
example.spot: Ananya does squats and push-ups at 6 pm,
example.feedback: The squats and push-ups are the signal. The meal then brings the parts to build with.

guided.stem: Kiran drinks a protein shake daily but never trains. What is he missing?
guided.hint: Food is one half of the pair.

options.text: The training signal.
options.feedback: Yes. Without strength work, the body does not use the protein to build muscle.

options.text: A second shake each day.
options.feedback: More protein cannot stand in for training. The signal to build is what is missing.

options.text: More rest days, so the shake can work.
options.feedback: Protein alone is not used for muscle building. Strength work gives the signal.

steps.takeaway: Training gives the signal; protein gives the parts.

steps.title: More protein is not more muscle

hook.stem: Does eating twice as much protein build twice as much muscle?

options.text: No, muscle can only use so much.
options.feedback: Right. Past a point, extra protein added no more muscle, even with strength training.

options.text: Yes, more protein means more muscle.
options.feedback: Muscle can use only so much. Above about 1.6 g per kilo a day, no extra gain showed up.

options.text: Yes, if most of it comes from powder.
options.feedback: Powder is just protein. Past about 1.6 g per kilo a day, more added no muscle.

steps.teach: Healthy adults need about 0.83 g of protein per kilo a day. Above about 1.6 g, training added no more muscle, since muscle uses only so much. With kidney disease, take care with high protein.

visual.label: Protein per kilo of body weight a day

marks.text: 1.6 g: no extra muscle above this

parts: Rohit weighs 60 kg and lifts weights,
so about 50 g of protein a day meets his need,
from dal, curd and eggs.
example.spot: so about 50 g of protein a day meets his need,
example.feedback: 60 times 0.83 is about 50, so dal, curd and eggs can cover his day.

guided.stem: Meena weighs 70 kg and trains. Above about what daily amount does extra protein stop adding muscle?
guided.hint: Use the higher figure per kilo.

options.text: About 112 g.
options.feedback: Yes. 70 times 1.6 is 112, and more than that added no extra muscle.

options.text: About 58 g.
options.feedback: That is 70 times 0.83, her daily need. The point past which more adds nothing is higher.

options.text: About 1,600 g.
options.feedback: The decimal slipped. 70 times 1.6 is about 112 grams, not 1,600.

steps.takeaway: Healthy adults need about 0.83 g a kilo; more is not more muscle.

steps.title: Building goes on after the session

hook.stem: After a hard strength session, how long can the muscle-building process stay switched on?

options.text: Up to about two days.
options.feedback: Right. A review found it can stay raised for up to 48 hours after one session.

options.text: Just while you are lifting.
options.feedback: The process goes on well after the session ends, for up to about two days.

options.text: For about two weeks.
options.feedback: Two weeks is far too long. The review found up to about 48 hours.

steps.teach: The muscle-building process stays switched on after a session, for up to two days. Meals in that time feed it, so rest days are part of training. The rise was smaller in adults over 50.

parts: Ishita trains her legs hard on Monday evening,
eats dal and rice that night and on Tuesday,
and saves her next hard leg day for Thursday.
example.spot: and saves her next hard leg day for Thursday.
example.feedback: The building process can stay switched on for up to two days, so Thursday gives her legs that time.

guided.stem: Rhea trained her legs hard on Monday. Is Tuesday a good day for another hard leg session?
guided.hint: Think about what her legs are still doing.

options.text: Better to rest them while the building goes on.
options.feedback: Yes. Building can stay switched on for up to two days, so a rest or an arm day fits Tuesday.

options.text: Yes, if she eats extra protein to recover.
options.feedback: Extra protein does not speed it up. Building goes on for up to two days, so rest or train arms.

options.text: Yes, since building stops once the session ends.
options.feedback: Building does not stop at the gym door. It can stay switched on for up to two days.

steps.takeaway: The muscle-building process can stay on for up to two days.

concepts.title: Sleep and recovery
concepts.hook: A late exam night can make the next match feel harder and the canteen snack more tempting.
concepts.rule: Much of the body's repair happens in deep sleep, and adults are advised 7 to 9 hours. Short sleep can lower sports performance, most of all when you wake far too early, and it shifts hunger hormones.

claims.text: Deep sleep triggers a hormone that helps build muscle and repair cells and tissues in adults.
Experts advise adults to sleep 7 to 9 hours a night.
In a review of athletes, short-term sleep loss, often a single night, lowered sports performance. Losing the end of the night hurt most, and losing the start showed no clear drop.
With too little sleep, the hunger hormone ghrelin goes up and the fullness hormone leptin goes down, so you feel hungrier.

items.stem: A teammate cuts his sleep to fit in an extra late session, saying more training beats more sleep. What is missing?

options.text: Sleep is when much repair happens, so cutting it cuts recovery.
options.feedback: Deep sleep releases a hormone that helps build muscle and repair tissue, so an hour less sleep costs recovery.

options.text: Late sessions build more muscle than early ones.
options.feedback: The clock time of the session is not the point. Cutting sleep cuts the repair that follows training.

options.text: Sleep helps the brain but does little for muscle.
options.feedback: Deep sleep also releases a hormone that helps build muscle and repair tissue in adults.

items.stem: After a cricket match, Ravi has a scraped knee and an exam week of 4-hour nights. What might the short nights slow?

options.text: The repair of his scrape and his tired muscles.
options.feedback: Sleep helps repair cells and tissues, so short nights can slow healing outside the gym too.

options.text: Little, since a scrape heals the same either way.
options.feedback: Repair of cells and tissues happens a lot in deep sleep, so short nights can slow it.

options.text: His exam marks, but not his body.
options.feedback: His body pays too. Deep sleep is when much of the repair of tissue happens.

items.stem: Before a school football match, Tara goes to bed two hours late but wakes at her usual time. What did the review find for this pattern?

options.text: No clear drop in play, unlike an early wake.
options.feedback: Losing the start of the night showed no clear drop in the review. Waking far too early hurt the most.

options.text: The biggest drop of the three patterns.
options.feedback: The biggest drop came from waking far too early, not from going to bed late.

options.text: Losing the start of sleep hurts play most.
options.feedback: The review found no clear drop after losing the start. Losing the end of the night hurt most.

items.stem: Ishaan usually sleeps from 11 pm to 7 am. Before a bus trip, early waking cut his sleep to 6 hours. About what time did his alarm ring?

options.text: About 5 am.
options.feedback: 11 pm to 7 am is 8 hours, so 6 hours of sleep means waking about 2 hours early, near 5 am.

options.text: About 1 am.
options.feedback: That would leave him only 2 hours of sleep. Six hours from 11 pm ends near 5 am.

options.text: About 9 am.
options.feedback: That is later than his usual 7 am wake. He woke early, near 5 am.

items.stem: In exam week, Neel sleeps 5 hours a night in the hostel and keeps feeling hungry between meals. Which change goes after the cause?

options.text: Getting closer to 7 to 9 hours of sleep.
options.feedback: Short sleep tends to push ghrelin up and leptin down, so more sleep goes after a likely cause.

options.text: Keep five hours of sleep to lower hunger.
options.feedback: Short sleep raises the hunger hormone and lowers the fullness hormone. More sleep addresses that cause.

options.text: Studying even later at night.
options.feedback: Later nights cut sleep further, which would push his hunger up even more.

items.stem: After a short night, Pooja eats a big lunch but still wants more food. Which hormone change explains still wanting food after eating?

options.text: Leptin, the fullness hormone, is low.
options.feedback: Short sleep lowers leptin, which helps you feel full, so a big lunch satisfies her less.

options.text: Ghrelin, the hunger hormone, has dropped.
options.feedback: Ghrelin goes up after short sleep, not down, which pushes hunger higher.

options.text: Short sleep lowers the hunger hormone.
options.feedback: Short sleep raises ghrelin and lowers leptin. Low leptin helps explain why she still wants food.

steps.title: Sleep is when the body repairs

hook.stem: Why might a coach call sleep part of training?

options.text: The body does much of its repair while you sleep.
options.feedback: Right. Deep sleep releases a hormone that helps build muscle and repair tissue.

options.text: Sleep burns more energy than a workout.
options.feedback: Energy is not the reason. Deep sleep is when much of the body's repair happens.

concepts.title: Warm-up and injury myths
concepts.hook: A few easy moves before hard work can let breathing and pulse rise bit by bit.
concepts.rule: A warm-up is usually an easier version of the activity, slower or lighter, so heart rate and breathing rise bit by bit. Long still holds just before power work can dull it a little. Stretching showed no clear effect on overall injury rates, so it is no guarantee.

claims.text: A gradual warm-up raises heart rate and breathing; long still holds can slightly lower results in tests done soon after.

In a review, holding a stretch for 60 seconds or more per muscle cut results in tests a few minutes later by about 4.6%, against about 1.1% for shorter holds. With active moves after, no clear effect was seen.
Static stretching had no clear effect on overall injury rates, and range gains usually lasted under 30 minutes. The review still suggests stretching inside a warm-up that ends with active moves.

concepts.title: Heat and hydration
concepts.hook: An Ahmedabad noon can make an outdoor session feel harder than the same work on a cool day.
concepts.rule: In heat your body works to shed heat as well as move. Train in cooler hours, start slow, sip water and replace salt on long days, but do not force down big amounts. Dizziness, nausea or cramps mean stop and get cool; confusion is an emergency.

claims.text: Hot exercise can raise heat risk and fluid loss. Feeling dizzy, sick or headachy can be a warning.
In hot weather, train early or late when it is cooler, start slow and pick up the pace bit by bit, and drink more water than usual without waiting for thirst.
In the heat, sweat may reach 1 litre an hour, taking fluid and salt. Forcing water on someone who is not thirsty raises risk, and food is the easiest way to replace salt.
In heat, the body must move heat from the core to the skin, and heart rate and temperature rise as the body loses fluid. Heart, sugar and kidney conditions lower heat tolerance.
Dizziness, nausea, headache, cramps or feeling faint in the heat are signs to stop, get cool and sip water. Get medical help if you throw up, feel worse, or it lasts over an hour.
Confusion or passing out in the heat can mean heat stroke, an emergency: call for help, move the person somewhere cool, cool them, and give nothing to drink.

steps.title: Plan hot days: cooler hours and a slow start

hook.stem: Your team wants to practise on a hot day. Which plan is safer?

options.text: Early morning, starting slow, with water breaks.
options.feedback: Right. Cooler hours, a slow start and water breaks all cut heat strain.

options.text: Noon, at full speed from the very start.
options.feedback: Midday is the hottest time, and a fast start adds strain on top.

options.text: Noon, with no water breaks, to toughen up.
options.feedback: Skipping water in heat is dangerous, not tough. Drink more than usual on hot days.

steps.teach: In heat, your body works to shed heat as well as move, so the same run is harder. Train in the cool morning or evening and start slow. A heart, kidney or sugar condition? Ask your doctor first.

parts: In a Chennai summer, the school team
moves football practice to 6 am,
and brings big water bottles.
example.spot: moves football practice to 6 am,
example.feedback: Moving to the cooler early morning cuts heat strain before the sun gets strong.

guided.stem: Practice is fixed at 4 pm in May. What can still be changed?
guided.hint: The clock is fixed, but the plan is not.

options.text: Start slower and build up over the session.
options.feedback: Yes. When the time cannot move, a slow start that builds up gradually still cuts strain.

options.text: Push harder; heat builds toughness.
options.feedback: Heat adds strain, not a bonus. Start slow and build up.

options.text: Go hard early, before the heat tires you.
options.feedback: A hard start adds heat strain. Start slow and pick up the pace bit by bit.

steps.takeaway: Hot day: cooler hours and a slow start. Have a condition? See a doctor.

steps.title: Sweat takes water and salt out

hook.stem: In one hour of hard work in the heat, about how much sweat can you lose?

options.text: Up to about 1 litre.
options.feedback: Right. Sweat can reach about 1 litre an hour in the heat.

options.text: About a cup at most.
options.feedback: It can be far more than that. Sweat in the heat can reach about 1 litre an hour.

options.text: About 5 litres an hour.
options.feedback: That is far too much. The top rate is about 1 litre an hour.

steps.teach: In hot weather, sweat can reach about 1 litre an hour, and salt leaves with it. So sip water through the session, but never force down big amounts. On long sweaty days, salty food helps replace the salt.

visual.label: Sweat in one hour of hot work

marks.text: Up to about 1 L an hour

parts: Rohan plays two hours of cricket in the summer sun,
and may sweat out up to 2 litres,
so he sips water at every break.
example.spot: and may sweat out up to 2 litres,
example.feedback: At up to 1 litre an hour, two hours in the heat can mean up to 2 litres.

guided.stem: Which plan fits a 2-hour hot match?
guided.hint: Fluid goes out fast in the heat.

options.text: Sips at every break, and a salty snack after.
options.feedback: Yes. Regular sips replace sweat as it goes, and salty food replaces the salt.

options.text: Two big bottles gulped down at the end.
options.feedback: Gulping big amounts at once is not the fix. Sip through the match instead.

options.text: Force down a litre at each break.
options.feedback: Do not force big amounts. Sip at breaks, and replace salt with food.

steps.takeaway: Up to 1 litre of sweat an hour: sip often, replace salt.

steps.title: Warning signs mean stop and cool down

hook.stem: Midway through a hot run, you feel dizzy and sick. What is the safe move?

options.text: Stop and get to a cool place.
options.feedback: Right. Dizziness and nausea in the heat are signs to stop and cool down.

options.text: Push on and finish the run.
options.feedback: Pushing on adds more heat strain. These are signs to stop.

options.text: Slow down, but keep running home.
options.feedback: Running on, even slowly, keeps making heat. Stop and cool down first.

steps.teach: Dizziness, nausea, headache, cramps or feeling faint in heat mean stop, get cool and sip water, because heat illness can get worse. Throwing up, getting worse or over an hour? Get medical help. Confusion means call an ambulance.

example.spot: Riya suddenly feels dizzy and weak,

guided.stem: A teammate seems confused on a hot field. What comes first?
guided.hint: Think about how serious this sign is.

options.text: Call an ambulance and move them somewhere cool.
options.feedback: Yes. Confusion in heat can mean heat stroke, an emergency. Cool them with wet cloths and give them nothing to drink.

options.text: Give them a big bottle of cold water to gulp down.
options.feedback: With heat stroke, do not give them anything to drink. Call an ambulance and cool them down.

options.text: Sit them on the bench and keep playing.
options.feedback: Confusion is an emergency sign. Call an ambulance and cool them down right away.

steps.takeaway: Warning sign in heat? Stop and cool down. Confused? Call an ambulance.

concepts.title: Cardio zones and talk test
concepts.hook: A walk can feel easy while a run makes speech come in short bursts. Breath gives a clue to effort.
concepts.rule: Your voice shows effort: talk but not sing is moderate, only a few words is vigorous. On a 0 to 10 scale moderate is 5 or 6, and the scale is your own. After time off, start moderate and build up; pain or odd breathlessness means rest.

claims.text: As a rule of thumb, at moderate effort you can talk but not sing; at vigorous effort you cannot say more than a few words without pausing for breath.
On a 0 to 10 effort scale, where sitting is 0, moderate effort is a 5 or 6 and vigorous starts at 7 or 8.
Effort is personal: less fit people need more effort than fitter people to do the same activity.
People who are inactive should start with moderate effort and add minutes and days first, effort later. Shortness of breath, pain, nausea or headache are signs the body needs rest.
After a long time without exercise, it is wise to see a doctor before starting a programme. New symptoms while building up also need a doctor.

items.stem: A friend says if you can talk at all, the workout is too easy to count. What is not quite right?

options.text: Talk but no singing marks moderate effort.
options.feedback: Being able to talk but not sing is the sign of moderate effort, which is real exercise.

options.text: Silent workouts are the ones that count.
options.feedback: Silence is not the test. Moderate effort lets you talk, and it is real effort.

options.text: Talking means you are already at vigorous effort.
options.feedback: Vigorous effort leaves breath for just a few words. Talking, but not singing, means moderate.

items.stem: At the college fest, Mira dances hard but can still chat, though she cannot sing along. Which effort is that?

options.text: Moderate effort.
options.feedback: Talking but not singing marks moderate effort, on a dance floor as much as on a track.

options.text: Very light effort.
options.feedback: If she cannot sing, she is working harder than a light pace.

options.text: Vigorous effort.
options.feedback: Vigorous would leave her only a few words per breath. She can still chat.

items.stem: Two friends walk the same hill at the same speed. One rates it 3, the other 7. Why can both be right?

options.text: Effort depends on each person's fitness.
options.feedback: Less fit people need more effort for the same task, so the ratings can differ.

options.text: One of them must be wrong about it.
options.feedback: Both can be honest. The scale rates each person's own effort.

options.text: The same speed must feel equal to both.
options.feedback: Effort depends on each person's fitness. The same hill and speed can feel different.

items.stem: Cardio check: on a run you can say only a few words per breath. About what number is that on the 0 to 10 scale?

options.text: About 7.5.
options.feedback: A few words per breath is vigorous, and vigorous starts at 7 or 8 on the scale.

options.text: About 3.
options.feedback: A 3 is light effort, where you could easily talk. A few words means vigorous.

options.text: About 10.
options.feedback: 10 is your hardest. Vigorous effort starts lower, at 7 or 8.

items.stem: Back at college after a long break, Rohit's first jog leaves him gasping single words. What should he change?

options.text: Slow to a pace where he can talk.
options.feedback: Gasping single words means vigorous. After time off, a moderate pace he can talk through is the start.

options.text: Push on until it starts to feel easy.
options.feedback: Pushing hard after a break is a big jump. A moderate, talking pace comes first.

options.text: Run faster, so the session ends sooner.
options.feedback: More speed means more effort. After time off he should slow to a talking pace.

items.stem: How would you explain the safe order for building up after time off?

options.text: More minutes and days first, then more effort.
options.feedback: Add time and days at a moderate effort first. Raise the effort later, once that feels fine.

options.text: More effort first, then more minutes.
options.feedback: Effort comes last. Minutes and days rise first, at a moderate effort.

options.text: Minutes, days and effort at once, in week one.
options.feedback: Raising everything at once is a big jump. Minutes and days come first, effort later.

misconceptions.name: One speed fits all
misconceptions.correction: Effort is personal: less fit people need more effort for the same task.

misconceptions.name: Talking means too easy
misconceptions.correction: If you can talk but not sing, your effort is moderate.

misconceptions.name: Start hard to catch up on the missed weeks
misconceptions.correction: After time off, start moderate and add minutes and days before effort.

misconceptions.name: Talking means vigorous effort
misconceptions.correction: You can chat at a moderate effort. At a hard effort, you get out a few words, then need a breath.

steps.title: New to it? Start moderate, then build

hook.stem: After months without exercise, which effort should your first sessions aim for?

options.text: Moderate, where you can still talk.
options.feedback: Right. After time off, start at a moderate effort and build up gradually.

options.text: Vigorous, to catch up on the missed weeks.
options.feedback: Hard effort after time off raises injury risk. Start moderate and build up.

options.text: Your hardest, to test where you stand.

steps.teach: After time off, start at a moderate effort you can talk through, because big jumps raise injury risk. Add minutes and days first, effort later. Pain, odd breathlessness, nausea or headache mean rest.

guided.stem: Om starts jogging and gets a sharp pain in his knee. What should he do?
guided.hint: Think about what pain is telling his body.

options.text: Stop and rest it, and see a doctor if it stays.
options.feedback: Yes. Pain is a sign the body needs rest, and a new problem that stays needs a doctor.

options.text: Push through so the knee gets used to it.
options.feedback: Pain is a warning sign, not something to train through. Stop and rest.

options.text: Rest today, then do double tomorrow.

concepts.title: Food labels in India
concepts.hook: A mango drink can show big fruit on the front and still be mostly water and sugar. The back of the pack tells you.
concepts.rule: Total sugars count every sugar; added sugars are only those put in. A mixed food that stresses an ingredient in words or pictures must usually give its percentage. The %RDA line compares one serving with a reference adult day, such as 50 g of added sugar.

claims.text: Labels give nutrition per 100 g or 100 ml, or per pack for single-serve packs, with a serving size and the number of servings.
Ingredients on an Indian pack are listed from most to least by weight or volume, as at the time of making.
Labels show total sugars and added sugars as separate lines; added sugars are only the sugars put into the food.
The per serving %RDA on a label is worked out against an average adult day that includes 50 g of added sugar.
When a mixed food stresses an ingredient in words or pictures, the label must usually give its percentage. Spices and seasonings used for flavour, and serving-suggestion pictures, are left out.

items.stem: A friend says a drink with no added sugars is sugar-free. What is not quite right?

options.text: Its total sugars can still be high from fruit or milk.
options.feedback: Total sugars include the food's own sugars, so no added sugar does not mean no sugar.

options.text: Added sugars are left off the nutrition labels of Indian packs.
options.feedback: Indian labels do show added sugars, on a line of their own next to total sugars.

options.text: Fruit sugar does not count as sugar.
options.feedback: Fruit sugar is still sugar. It shows up in the total sugars line.

items.stem: A label shows 9 g total sugars and 9 g added sugars. What does that tell you about the food's own sugar?

options.text: None of its sugar comes from fruit or milk.
options.feedback: When added sugars equal total sugars, every gram was put in, and the food has none of its own.

options.text: It has 9 g of its own sugar on top.
options.feedback: Added sugars are part of the total, not extra. Equal lines mean all of it was added.

options.text: It has 18 g of sugar in total.
options.feedback: The total is already 9 g. The added line is part of that total, not on top of it.

items.stem: A masala chips pack shows chillies in its picture but gives no chilli %. Why can that be allowed?

options.text: Spices used for flavour are left out of the % rule.
options.feedback: The % rule has exceptions, and spices or seasonings used for flavour are one of them.

options.text: Ingredient percentages apply to drinks, not chips.
options.feedback: The percentage rule can apply to mixed foods. Spices used for flavour are an exception.

options.text: The % rule covers drinks, not snacks.
options.feedback: The rule covers mixed foods of many kinds. Spices used for flavour are the exception here.

items.stem: In the college canteen, a biscuit pack says 'with real honey' in big letters. What should its label show?

options.text: The share of honey in the biscuit, as a %.
options.feedback: Stressing an ingredient in words counts just like a picture, so its % has to be given.

options.text: A photo of the farm where the honey came from.
options.feedback: No farm photo is needed. Stressing honey in words means its % must be shown.

options.text: No %, because honey is natural.
options.feedback: Being natural does not matter. A stressed ingredient must show its share as a %.

items.stem: On a food label, a cereal serving has 18 g total sugars: 4 g are the milk's own, and the rest were added. About what %RDA for added sugar should it show?

options.text: About 28%.
options.feedback: Added sugar is 18 minus 4, which is 14 g, and 14 out of the 50 g reference is 28%.

options.text: About 36%.
options.feedback: That uses all 18 g. Only the added part counts: 14 g out of 50 g is 28%.

options.text: About 8%.
options.feedback: That uses the 4 g from milk. The added part is 14 g, which is 28% of the reference.

items.stem: At the hostel shop, Kiran eats two servings of a snack whose label shows 12% for added sugar per serving. About what share of the reference day is that?

options.text: About 24%.
options.feedback: The %RDA is per serving, so two servings double it to about 24%.

options.text: About 12%.
options.feedback: 12% is for one serving. Two servings double it to about 24%.

options.text: About 48%.
options.feedback: That is four servings. Two servings of 12% make about 24%.

misconceptions.correction: A stressed ingredient's % on the label shows how much is really there.

misconceptions.name: %RDA is for the whole pack

misconceptions.correction: Added sugars are part of total sugars, not an extra amount.
